questions.q: Who were the first Europeans to explore Canada, about 1,000 years ago?
questions.e: The Vikings from Iceland, who colonized Greenland 1,000 years ago, also reached Labrador and the island of Newfoundland.

questions.q: Where can you see the remains of the Vikings' settlement in Canada?
questions.e: The remains of the Vikings' settlement at L'Anse aux Meadows, Newfoundland and Labrador, are a World Heritage Site.

questions.q: Who was the first explorer to draw a map of Canada's Atlantic shore, in 1497?
questions.e: John Cabot, an Italian immigrant to England, was the first to map Canada's Atlantic shore, setting foot on Newfoundland or Cape Breton Island in 1497 and claiming the new-found-land for England.

questions.q: John Cabot was an Italian immigrant to England.
questions.e: John Cabot, an Italian immigrant to England, mapped Canada's Atlantic shore in 1497 and claimed the land for England.

questions.q: When did English settlement begin in Newfoundland?
questions.e: English settlement did not begin until 1610, more than a century after John Cabot's voyage.

questions.q: Who made three voyages across the Atlantic between 1534 and 1542 and claimed the land for the King of France?
questions.e: Between 1534 and 1542, Jacques Cartier made three voyages across the Atlantic, claiming the land for King Francis I of France.

questions.q: Where does the name 'Canada' come from?
questions.a: From 'kanata', an Iroquoian word meaning village
w: From a French word meaning cold land
From the name of an English king
From an Inuit word meaning our land
questions.e: Jacques Cartier heard two captured guides speak the Iroquoian word 'kanata', meaning 'village'. By the 1550s the name of Canada began appearing on maps.

questions.q: For which French King did Jacques Cartier claim the land?
questions.e: Jacques Cartier claimed the land for King Francis I of France.

questions.q: By the 1550s, the name 'Canada' began appearing on maps.
questions.e: The word 'kanata' (village) gave Canada its name, which began appearing on maps in the 1550s.

questions.q: In 1604, who established the first European settlement north of Florida?
questions.a: Pierre de Monts and Samuel de Champlain
w: James Wolfe and the Marquis de Montcalm
questions.e: In 1604, the first European settlement north of Florida was established by French explorers Pierre de Monts and Samuel de Champlain, first on St. Croix Island and then at Port-Royal in Acadia (present-day Nova Scotia).

questions.q: Who built a fortress at what is now Quebec City in 1608?
questions.e: In 1608 Samuel de Champlain built a fortress at what is now Quebec City.

questions.q: With which Aboriginal peoples did the French colonists make alliances?
questions.e: Champlain allied the colony with the Algonquin, Montagnais and Huron, historic enemies of the Iroquois.

questions.q: The French colonists fought wars with the Iroquois.
questions.e: The colonists fought the Iroquois for 100 years, until peace was made in 1701.

questions.q: What was the economy of New France mainly based on?
questions.e: The French and Aboriginal people collaborated in the vast fur-trade economy, driven by the demand for beaver pelts in Europe.

questions.q: What were the French fur traders who travelled by canoe called?
questions.e: Outstanding leaders like Jacques Marquette, Robert Cavelier de La Salle, Pierre Le Moyne d'Iberville and Antoine Laumet dit de Lamothe Cadillac extended New France. Voyageurs and coureurs des bois carried the fur trade by canoe.

questions.q: In 1670, King Charles II of England granted exclusive trading rights over the lands draining into Hudson Bay to which company?
questions.e: In 1670, King Charles II granted the Hudson's Bay Company exclusive trading rights over the watershed draining into Hudson Bay.

questions.q: The Hudson's Bay Company competed with fur traders based in Montreal.
questions.e: For the next 100 years the Hudson's Bay Company competed with Montreal-based traders.

questions.q: In 1759, the British defeated the French in which battle at Quebec City?
questions.a: The Battle of the Plains of Abraham
questions.e: In 1759, the British defeated the French in the Battle of the Plains of Abraham at Quebec City, marking the end of France's empire in America.

questions.q: Which two commanders were killed in the Battle of the Plains of Abraham?
questions.a: Brigadier James Wolfe and the Marquis de Montcalm
w: Sir John A. Macdonald and Louis Riel
Samuel de Champlain and Jacques Cartier
questions.e: The commanders of both armies, Brigadier James Wolfe and the Marquis de Montcalm, were killed leading their troops in battle.

questions.q: The Battle of the Plains of Abraham marked the end of France's empire in America.
questions.e: The British victory in 1759 ended France's empire in America.

questions.q: After the war with France, what did Great Britain name the colony?
questions.e: Following the war, Great Britain renamed the colony the 'Province of Quebec'.

questions.q: What did the Quebec Act of 1774 do?
questions.a: It allowed religious freedom for Catholics and restored French civil law
w: It made English the only language in Quebec
It created the Dominion of Canada
It gave women the right to vote
questions.e: The Quebec Act of 1774 allowed religious freedom for Catholics and permitted them to hold public office. It restored French civil law while keeping British criminal law.

questions.q: The French-speaking Catholic people of the Province of Quebec were called what?
questions.e: The French-speaking Catholic people, called habitants or Canadiens, wanted to keep their way of life.

questions.q: Who were the United Empire Loyalists?
questions.a: People who stayed loyal to the Crown and left the United States after it declared independence in 1776
w: French settlers who came to Acadia in 1604
Soldiers who fought at Vimy Ridge
Fur traders of the Hudson's Bay Company
questions.e: In 1776, the 13 British colonies south of Quebec declared independence. More than 40,000 people loyal to the Crown, called Loyalists, fled to Quebec and Nova Scotia.

questions.q: About how many Loyalists fled to Quebec and Nova Scotia?
questions.e: More than 40,000 Loyalists fled the oppression of the American Revolution to settle in Quebec and Nova Scotia.

questions.q: Who led thousands of Loyalist Mohawk Indians into Canada?
questions.e: Joseph Brant led thousands of Loyalist Mohawk Indians into Canada.

questions.q: The Loyalists came from many backgrounds, including Dutch, German, British, Scandinavian, Aboriginal and others.
questions.e: The Loyalists came from Dutch, German, British, Scandinavian, Aboriginal and other origins, and from Presbyterian, Anglican, Baptist, Methodist, Jewish, Quaker and Catholic religious backgrounds. About 3,000 Black Loyalists came too.

questions.q: Where was the first representative assembly in Canada elected, in 1758?
questions.e: The first representative assembly was elected in Halifax, Nova Scotia, in 1758. Prince Edward Island followed in 1773 and New Brunswick in 1785.

questions.q: The Constitutional Act of 1791 divided the Province of Quebec into which two colonies?
questions.e: The Constitutional Act of 1791 divided the Province of Quebec into Upper Canada (later Ontario), which was mainly Loyalist, Protestant and English-speaking, and Lower Canada (later Quebec), which was Catholic and French-speaking.

questions.q: Upper Canada later became which province?
questions.e: Upper Canada became Ontario and Lower Canada became Quebec.

questions.q: The Constitutional Act of 1791 gave Upper and Lower Canada legislative assemblies elected by the people.
questions.e: The Act granted legislative assemblies elected by the people for the first time. The name Canada also became official at this time.

questions.q: When did the name 'Canada' become official?
questions.e: The name Canada became official with the Constitutional Act of 1791.

questions.q: Which colony was the first province in the British Empire to move toward abolishing slavery, in 1793?
questions.e: In 1793, Upper Canada, led by Lieutenant Governor John Graves Simcoe, became the first province in the Empire to move toward abolition.

questions.q: Who was the Lieutenant Governor of Upper Canada who moved to abolish slavery and founded the city of Toronto?
questions.e: Lieutenant Governor John Graves Simcoe, the founder of the City of Toronto, led Upper Canada toward the abolition of slavery in 1793.

questions.q: When did the British Parliament abolish slavery throughout the British Empire?
questions.e: In 1833 the British Parliament abolished slavery throughout the Empire.

questions.q: What was the Underground Railroad?
questions.a: A network that helped thousands of slaves escape from the United States to Canada
w: The first railway built across Canada
A route used by fur traders
questions.e: Thousands of slaves escaped from the United States, followed 'the North Star' and settled in Canada via the Underground Railroad, a Christian anti-slavery network.

questions.q: Who was a Black anti-slavery activist and the first woman publisher in Canada?
questions.e: Mary Ann Shadd Cary was an outspoken activist in the abolition movement and became the first woman publisher in Canada.

questions.q: In what year did the first stock exchange in Canada open, in Montreal?
questions.e: The first companies in Canada were formed during the French and British regimes and competed for the fur trade. In 1832 the Montreal Stock Exchange opened.

questions.q: What happened in the War of 1812?
questions.a: The United States invaded Canada and was defeated
w: The Hudson's Bay Company was created
questions.e: In 1812 the United States invaded Canada, believing it would be easy to conquer. Canadian volunteers, British soldiers and First Nations fought together and defended Canada.

questions.q: Who captured Detroit in the War of 1812 but was killed defending Queenston Heights?
questions.e: Major-General Sir Isaac Brock captured Detroit but was killed while defending against an American attack at Queenston Heights, near Niagara Falls.

questions.q: Which First Nations leader fought with the British and Canadians in the War of 1812?
questions.e: Led by Shawnee Chief Tecumseh, First Nations fought alongside Canadian volunteers and British soldiers.

questions.q: Who led about 460 soldiers, mostly French Canadians, to turn back 4,000 American invaders at Châteauguay in 1813?
questions.e: In 1813, Lieutenant-Colonel Charles de Salaberry and 460 soldiers, mostly French Canadians, turned back 4,000 American invaders at Châteauguay, south of Montreal.

questions.q: Who walked 30 km (19 miles) in 1813 to warn Lieutenant James FitzGibbon of an American attack?
questions.e: In 1813, Laura Secord walked 19 miles (30 km) to warn Lieutenant James FitzGibbon of a planned American attack. Her bravery contributed to victory at the Battle of Beaver Dams.

questions.q: In 1814, a British expedition from Nova Scotia burned down the White House in Washington, D.C.
questions.e: In 1814, Major-General Robert Ross led an expedition from Nova Scotia that burned down the White House and other public buildings in Washington, D.C.

questions.q: The War of 1812 helped to shape the border between Canada and the United States.
questions.e: By 1814 the American attempt to conquer Canada had failed. Canada's present-day border is partly an outcome of the War of 1812.

questions.q: Canada lost the War of 1812 and became part of the United States.
questions.e: The American invasion failed. Canada remained independent of the United States, and the war helped build Canada's sense of identity.

questions.q: In 1837–38, rebellions took place in which colonies?
questions.e: In 1837–38, small groups of rebels in Upper and Lower Canada believed the progress to full democracy was too slow.

questions.q: Who recommended that Upper and Lower Canada be merged and given responsible government?
questions.e: Lord Durham, an English reformer sent to report on the rebellions, recommended that Upper and Lower Canada be merged and given responsible government.

questions.q: In what year were Upper and Lower Canada united as the Province of Canada?
questions.e: In 1840, Upper and Lower Canada were united as the Province of Canada.

questions.q: What is responsible government?
questions.a: The ministers of the Crown must have the support of a majority of the elected representatives to govern
w: The King makes all decisions without Parliament
questions.e: Responsible government means the ministers of the Crown must have the support of a majority of the elected representatives in order to govern.

questions.q: Which was the first British North American colony to get full responsible government, in 1847–48?
questions.e: Nova Scotia was the first British North American colony to attain full responsible government, in 1847–48.

questions.q: Who was the first head of a responsible government in Canada, in 1849?
questions.e: Sir Louis-Hippolyte La Fontaine, a champion of democracy and French language rights, became the first head of a responsible government (similar to a prime minister) in Canada in 1849.

questions.q: Responsible government was introduced in Nova Scotia and the Province of Canada in the late 1840s.
questions.e: Nova Scotia got full responsible government in 1847–48, and the Province of Canada followed in 1848–49 under La Fontaine and Robert Baldwin.

questions.q: In what year did Confederation take place?
questions.e: In 1867, the Dominion of Canada was officially born.

questions.q: Which four provinces formed Canada at Confederation in 1867?
questions.a: Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick
w: Ontario, Quebec, Manitoba and British Columbia
Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland
questions.e: The Dominion of Canada was formed in 1867 by Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick.

questions.q: Who were the Fathers of Confederation?
questions.a: Representatives who worked from 1864 to 1867 to create a new country
w: The first fur traders in Canada
The first Canadian soldiers in the First World War
The founders of the Hudson's Bay Company
questions.e: From 1864 to 1867, representatives of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and the Province of Canada, with British support, worked together to establish a new country. They are known as the Fathers of Confederation.

questions.q: The Fathers of Confederation created two levels of government. What are they?
questions.e: The Fathers of Confederation created two levels of government: federal and provincial.

questions.q: What was the British North America Act of 1867 later renamed?
w: The Charter of Rights and Freedoms
questions.e: The British North America Act, 1867, which created the Dominion of Canada, is now called the Constitution Act, 1867.

questions.q: Who suggested the term 'Dominion of Canada' in 1864?
questions.e: Sir Leonard Tilley, a Father of Confederation from New Brunswick, suggested the term Dominion of Canada in 1864, inspired by Psalm 72 of the Bible.

questions.q: July 1 used to be called Dominion Day and is now called Canada Day.
questions.e: July 1 was celebrated as Dominion Day starting in 1879 and was officially renamed Canada Day in 1982.

questions.q: Who was Canada's first Prime Minister?
questions.e: Sir John Alexander Macdonald, a Father of Confederation, became Canada's first Prime Minister.

questions.q: Where was Sir John A. Macdonald born?
questions.e: Sir John A. Macdonald was born in Scotland on January 11, 1815, and came to Upper Canada as a child.

questions.q: Who was a key architect of Confederation from Quebec?
questions.e: Sir George-Étienne Cartier was the key architect of Confederation from Quebec. He led Quebec into Confederation and helped negotiate the entry of the Northwest Territories, Manitoba and British Columbia.

questions.q: In which year did Manitoba join Canada?
questions.e: Manitoba and the Northwest Territories became part of Canada in 1870.

questions.q: In which year did British Columbia join Canada?
questions.e: British Columbia joined Canada in 1871, after Ottawa promised to build a railway to the West Coast.

questions.q: In which year did Prince Edward Island join Canada?
questions.e: Prince Edward Island joined Canada in 1873.

questions.q: Which two provinces joined Canada in 1905?
questions.e: Alberta and Saskatchewan became provinces in 1905.

questions.q: Which was the last province to join Canada, in 1949?
questions.e: Newfoundland and Labrador joined Canada in 1949.

questions.q: In which year did Yukon become a territory?
questions.e: The Yukon Territory was created in 1898, during the Klondike Gold Rush.

questions.q: Which promise brought British Columbia into Confederation?
questions.a: A railway to the West Coast
w: A new capital city in Vancouver
questions.e: British Columbia joined Canada in 1871 after Ottawa promised to build a railway to the West Coast.

questions.q: Who led the Métis in the Red River Rebellion of 1869 and later in the North West Rebellion of 1885?
questions.e: Louis Riel led the Métis uprisings. In 1869 he seized Fort Garry, the territorial capital. He was tried and executed for high treason after the 1885 rebellion in present-day Saskatchewan.

questions.q: What led to the creation of the province of Manitoba?
questions.a: The Red River Rebellion led by Louis Riel
w: The building of the Rideau Canal
questions.e: Ottawa negotiated with the Métis after the Red River Rebellion, and in 1870 the province of Manitoba was created.

questions.q: Louis Riel is seen by many as a hero who defended Métis rights.
questions.e: Many people see Riel as a hero, a defender of Métis rights and the father of Manitoba.

questions.q: In 1873, Sir John A. Macdonald established which police force to bring order to the West?
questions.e: In 1873, Prime Minister Macdonald established the North West Mounted Police (NWMP) to pacify the West and help negotiations with the First Nations.

questions.q: What is the North West Mounted Police called today?
questions.e: The NWMP later became the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP), the national police force. The 'Mounties' are a popular symbol of Canada.

questions.q: Who was a famous Mountie who helped keep order during the Klondike Gold Rush?
questions.e: Sir Sam Steele was a great frontier hero, Mounted Policeman and soldier of the Queen.

questions.q: In what year was the Canadian Pacific Railway completed?
questions.e: The Canadian Pacific Railway was completed in 1885. The 'last spike' was driven in British Columbia on November 7, 1885.

questions.q: Who did much of the dangerous work of building the Canadian Pacific Railway in British Columbia?
questions.e: The railway was built by European and Chinese labour. After it was completed, the federal government put a 'head tax' on Chinese immigrants. Ottawa apologized for this policy in 2006.

questions.q: The Government of Canada apologized in 2006 for the Chinese head tax.
questions.e: After the railway was built, a head tax was placed on Chinese immigrants. The Government of Canada apologized for this discriminatory policy in 2006.

questions.q: The Canadian Pacific Railway helped to unite Canada from sea to sea.
questions.e: The railway was a great engineering achievement that linked the country from coast to coast and helped settle the West.

questions.q: Who was the first French-Canadian Prime Minister since Confederation?
questions.e: Sir Wilfrid Laurier became the first French-Canadian prime minister since Confederation and encouraged Canadians to unite. His portrait is on the $5 bill.

questions.q: Whose portrait is on the Canadian $5 bill?
questions.e: Sir Wilfrid Laurier, Canada's first French-Canadian prime minister since Confederation, is on the $5 bill.

questions.q: Many immigrants, including Ukrainians, Poles and Germans, helped settle the Prairies in the late 1800s and early 1900s.
questions.e: Between 1890 and 1914 a wave of immigrants from Europe, including Ukrainians, Poles, Germans, Dutch and Scandinavians, settled and farmed the Prairies.

questions.q: About how many Canadians volunteered to fight in the South African War (Boer War) of 1899–1902?
questions.e: More than 7,000 Canadians, including women nurses, volunteered to fight in the South African War, also called the Boer War.

questions.q: Jacques Cartier claimed the land for the King of England.
questions.e: Jacques Cartier claimed the land for King Francis I of France. John Cabot claimed land for England.

questions.q: Samuel de Champlain founded Montreal in 1608.
questions.e: In 1608 Samuel de Champlain built a fortress at what is now Quebec City.

questions.q: The Quebec Act of 1774 banned the Catholic religion in Quebec.
questions.e: The Quebec Act of 1774 allowed religious freedom for Catholics and restored French civil law.

questions.q: Laura Secord warned the Americans about a British attack.
questions.e: Laura Secord walked 30 km to warn the British, Lieutenant James FitzGibbon, of a planned American attack.

questions.q: Confederation in 1867 joined all ten provinces together.
questions.e: Only four provinces formed Canada in 1867: Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. The others joined later, the last in 1949.

questions.q: Alberta and Saskatchewan were among the first four provinces of Canada in 1867.
questions.e: Alberta and Saskatchewan became provinces in 1905.

questions.q: Louis Riel was the first Prime Minister of Canada.
questions.e: Sir John A. Macdonald was the first Prime Minister. Louis Riel led the Métis uprisings of 1869 and 1885.
